ai.definition: Quantum Computing Beyond 2035 refers to the development of highly advanced quantum computing systems that are capable of handling complex computations with a high degree of accuracy and reliability. This includes the creation of fault-tolerant quantum computers and the establishment of robust quantum internet infrastructure.
ai.howItWorks: These advancements rely on improvements in qubit error correction techniques, which help to mitigate errors caused by environmental factors and physical limitations. Additionally, network protocols are being developed to ensure secure and efficient data transmission over quantum networks.
ai.problemSolved: The current limitations of quantum computers, such as susceptibility to noise and decoherence, are addressed through these advancements. This enables the execution of more complex algorithms and tasks that require high computational power.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing processes will involve the creation of highly specialized components, including advanced qubits with improved stability and error correction mechanisms. The assembly of these components into functional quantum computers will also require precise engineering techniques.
ai.buildProcess: The build process involves rigorous testing and validation to ensure that each component meets the required standards for performance and reliability. This includes extensive simulations and real-world tests under various conditions.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include the development of new materials, the complexity of manufacturing processes, and the need for specialized equipment. Research and development expenses will also be significant due to the cutting-edge nature of the technology.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook suggests that these technologies are expected to transition from research and development into early commercial stages within the next decade, with gradual adoption in specialized industries.
ai.regulation: Regulatory frameworks will need to be established or updated to address the unique aspects of quantum computing, such as security concerns and potential misuse. This includes developing standards for data protection and privacy in quantum networks.
ai.risks: Technical risks include the ongoing challenges of scaling qubits while maintaining coherence. Security risks arise from the potential vulnerabilities of quantum systems, which could be exploited by malicious actors.
ai.profitability: Profitability is expected to increase as more industries recognize the value of advanced computing capabilities and secure communication channels provided by quantum technologies. However, initial costs may limit widespread adoption in the short term.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development will focus on further refining qubit technology, enhancing network protocols for quantum internet, and expanding applications across various sectors such as cryptography, drug discovery, and optimization problems.

glossary.def: The basic unit of quantum information, analogous to a classical bit but capable of existing in multiple states simultaneously.
A phenomenon where the state of a qubit becomes entangled with its environment, leading to loss of coherence and increased error rates.
A network that uses quantum communication protocols for secure data transmission between quantum computers and other nodes.

subsystems.name: Qubit chip
subsystems.role: stores and manipulates quantum states in a physical device.
parts: superconducting transmons, trapped ions, neutral atoms or photonic circuits

subsystems.name: Error-correction layer
subsystems.role: combines many noisy physical qubits into a few reliable logical qubits.
parts: real-time decoder on FPGAs or custom chips

subsystems.name: Control and cryogenics
subsystems.role: keeps qubits cold and quiet, and delivers precise pulses.

subsystems.name: Quantum interconnect
subsystems.role: entangles separate processors and distant nodes.

subsystems.name: Software stack
subsystems.role: turns an algorithm into error-corrected pulse sequences.

subsystems.name: Classical co-processing
subsystems.role: runs the parts of a job a quantum machine cannot do.
parts: secure key-management nodes for quantum links

buildSteps.title: Fabricate qubit chips
buildSteps.detail: Josephson junctions and resonators are patterned on silicon or sapphire in a nanofabrication cleanroom, then diced and packaged.

buildSteps.title: Wire and cool the processor
buildSteps.detail: the chip is mounted in a dilution refrigerator at a few thousandths of a kelvin, with filtered cabling that carries signals without adding heat or noise.

buildSteps.title: Calibrate the gates
buildSteps.detail: each qubit's frequency, pulse amplitudes and two-qubit gate timings are tuned by automated routines that measure fidelity thousands of times.

buildSteps.title: Encode a logical qubit
buildSteps.detail: many physical qubits are entangled into one error-corrected logical qubit, and error 'syndromes' are measured repeatedly without collapsing the stored state.

buildSteps.title: Decode in real time
buildSteps.detail: a classical decoder inspects the syndrome stream fast enough — microseconds — to correct errors before they accumulate.

buildSteps.title: Scale to many logical qubits
buildSteps.detail: more logical qubits are added, either on larger chips or by linking smaller modules through photonic interconnects.

buildSteps.title: Build network nodes
buildSteps.detail: to go beyond one machine, entanglement is generated between distant nodes, stored in quantum memories and swapped through repeaters to extend range.

buildSteps.title: Run applications at scale
buildSteps.detail: fault-tolerant machines are coupled to classical supercomputers for chemistry, materials and cryptanalysis workloads; separate quantum key distribution links already carry secure keys between pilot sites.

prerequisites.why: two-qubit gate fidelities near or above 99.9% are needed before error correction pays off, and only some platforms reach this.
a 2024 superconducting experiment showed logical errors shrinking as more physical qubits were added, but at very small scale.
today's wiring and electronics would swamp a machine with millions of qubits; multiplexed cryogenic control is still being developed.
a quantum internet needs to store and relay entanglement over long distances, which has not been done at useful rates.
linking superconducting processors over fibre requires converting quantum states between microwave and optical frequencies with high efficiency.

pathway.milestone: processors with roughly a hundred to a few hundred physical qubits and early logical-qubit demonstrations
pathway.unlocks: benchmarks, calibration know-how and the first error-corrected memory experiments.

pathway.milestone: early fault tolerance: hundreds of logical qubits with errors suppressed below what any classical simulation can track
pathway.unlocks: small but genuinely useful quantum chemistry and optimisation runs.

pathway.milestone: fault-tolerant machines with thousands of logical qubits, plus metropolitan entanglement links between a handful of nodes
pathway.unlocks: practical catalyst and materials design; device-independent secure communication over city distances.

pathway.milestone: modular, networked quantum computers and repeater-based long-distance quantum networks
pathway.unlocks: distributed quantum computing and a genuine quantum internet — conditional on solving transduction, memory and control-scaling problems.
